CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the principles of experimental design as applied to controlled usability testing.
Identify appropriate participant selection criteria and recruitment strategies for usability studies.
Apply task scenario scripting techniques to create realistic and measurable usability test tasks.
Demonstrate the think-aloud protocol by facilitating a live user testing session.
Analyze both quantitative and qualitative data collected during usability testing sessions.
Create a structured results report compiling findings from team-conducted user testing sessions.

Topics.Title: Foundations of Experimental Design for Usability Testing
Topics.Summary: Introduces the core principles of experimental design and how they apply to planning and structuring controlled usability tests. Covers key variables, controls, and study validity considerations.

Elements.Title: What Is Experimental Design in Usability Testing?
Elements.BodyText: Experimental design in usability testing is the systematic planning of a study to ensure results are valid, reliable, and actionable. It defines what will be tested, how it will be measured, and how variables will be controlled.
Elements.Notes: Emphasize to students that poor experimental design can invalidate all data collected, no matter how well the session itself is run. Draw parallels to scientific experiments to ground the concept.

Items.Text: Experimental design establishes the structure and rules of a usability study before any sessions begin.
A well-designed study controls for extraneous variables that could distort results.
Usability studies can follow within-subjects or between-subjects designs depending on research goals.
Defining clear research questions at the outset guides all subsequent design decisions.

Elements.Title: Independent and Dependent Variables
Elements.BodyText: In a usability study, the independent variable is the condition being manipulated (such as interface version), while the dependent variables are the outcomes being measured (such as task completion time or error rate).
Elements.Notes: A common student error is confusing participant characteristics with independent variables. Clarify that participant traits are often moderating variables, not the primary manipulated condition.

Items.Text: The independent variable is deliberately changed or varied by the researcher to observe its effect.
Dependent variables are the measurable outcomes that reflect user performance or experience.
Clearly labeling variables before testing prevents ambiguity during data collection.
Multiple dependent variables can be measured in a single session to capture a fuller picture of usability.

Elements.Title: Study Validity: Internal and External
Elements.BodyText: Internal validity refers to the degree to which the study accurately measures what it intends to, while external validity refers to how well the findings generalize to real-world contexts.
Elements.Notes: Lab-based usability tests often trade some external validity for greater internal control. Discuss this trade-off with students and how field studies or remote testing can complement lab findings.

Items.Text: Internal validity is threatened by confounds, experimenter bias, or inconsistent procedures.
External validity depends on how representative the participants and tasks are of the real user population.
Standardizing session procedures is one of the most effective ways to protect internal validity.
Pilot testing helps identify threats to validity before the main study is conducted.

Elements.Title: Choosing a Study Type: Formative vs. Summative
Elements.BodyText: Formative usability tests are conducted during development to identify and fix problems, while summative tests are conducted after development to evaluate the overall quality of a finished product.
Elements.Notes: Most student team projects in this module will use a formative approach since they are testing prototypes or early-stage designs. However, introduce summative testing so students understand both contexts.

Items.Text: Formative testing is exploratory and iterative, prioritizing problem discovery over measurement.
Summative testing is evaluative and often benchmarks performance against standards or competitors.
The choice of study type influences participant sample size, task design, and data collection methods.
Both types can be combined in a single project at different phases of development.

Elements.Title: Ethical Considerations in Usability Studies
Elements.BodyText: Conducting usability testing involves ethical responsibilities including informed consent, participant confidentiality, the right to withdraw, and data handling practices.
Elements.Notes: Require students to draft an informed consent form as part of their study setup. Reference any applicable institutional review policies. Remind teams that participants are volunteers, not test subjects in a punishing sense.

Items.Text: All participants must provide informed consent before any testing begins.
Participants have the right to stop the session at any time without penalty.
Collected data must be anonymized or de-identified to protect participant privacy.
Teams must explain the purpose of the study at a level participants can understand.

Topics.Title: Participant Selection and Recruitment
Topics.Summary: Addresses how to define the target user population, establish inclusion and exclusion criteria, and recruit an appropriate sample of participants for a usability study.

Elements.Title: Defining the Target User Population
Elements.BodyText: The target user population is the group of people for whom the product is designed, and all participant selection decisions should reflect meaningful characteristics of this group.
Elements.Notes: Encourage students to revisit any personas or user research from earlier in their project to ground their population definition in prior evidence rather than assumptions.

Items.Text: The target population is defined by shared characteristics relevant to the product's use context.
Demographic, behavioral, and experiential attributes all contribute to population definition.
A clear population definition prevents recruiting participants who are not representative of real users.
Population definition should be documented in the study plan before recruitment begins.

Elements.Title: Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
Elements.BodyText: Inclusion criteria specify the characteristics a participant must have to qualify for the study, while exclusion criteria identify characteristics that would disqualify a candidate.
Elements.Notes: Common exclusion criteria include prior familiarity with the specific product being tested, employment in UX or software development fields, or sensory or cognitive impairments that would prevent meaningful task completion unless the product is designed for those users.

Items.Text: Inclusion criteria ensure that participants genuinely represent the intended user group.
Exclusion criteria reduce bias from participants with atypical prior knowledge or experience.
Both types of criteria must be applied consistently across all recruitment screening.
Overly restrictive criteria can make recruitment difficult and reduce sample diversity.

Elements.Title: Screening and Recruitment Methods
Elements.BodyText: Screening involves vetting potential participants against selection criteria, typically using a screener survey or questionnaire administered before the study begins.
Elements.Notes: Avoid leading screener questions that might signal the 'correct' answer to participants. For example, don't ask 'Do you frequently shop online?' if you want online shoppers — instead ask about frequency in a neutral way.

Items.Text: A screener survey is the primary tool for verifying that candidates meet inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Recruitment channels include social media, campus networks, professional associations, and participant panels.
Incentives such as gift cards or course credit can improve recruitment rates and reduce attrition.
Screener results should be documented to create an audit trail of the selection process.

Elements.Title: Sample Size Considerations
Elements.BodyText: Determining how many participants to recruit depends on the study type, the diversity of the user population, and the depth of insights needed.
Elements.Notes: The Nielsen heuristic of five participants per user group is commonly cited for formative studies, but this is a guideline, not a rule. For summative or quantitative studies, larger samples are needed for statistical power. Discuss this nuance with students.

Items.Text: Formative usability studies often use five to eight participants per distinct user group to identify the most critical problems.
Summative and quantitative studies require larger samples to produce statistically meaningful results.
Recruiting more participants than needed as backups helps offset no-shows or disqualifications.
Homogeneous populations may require fewer participants than highly diverse ones to achieve saturation.

Elements.Title: Scheduling and Logistics
Elements.BodyText: Participant scheduling involves coordinating session times, confirming locations or remote access links, and communicating all logistical details to participants in advance.
Elements.Notes: Build buffer time between sessions to allow the team to reset the test environment, debrief, and prepare for the next participant. A minimum of 15 minutes between sessions is recommended.

Items.Text: Confirmation emails should be sent immediately after scheduling and again 24 hours before the session.
Session length estimates should be realistic and communicated clearly to participants.
Remote sessions require pre-testing of all technology to prevent session-day failures.
A point-of-contact name and number should be provided so participants can reach the team if needed.

Topics.Title: Task Scenario Scripting
Topics.Summary: Covers the design and writing of realistic, measurable task scenarios that guide participants through the usability test while eliciting meaningful behavioral data.

Elements.Title: What Makes a Good Task Scenario?
Elements.BodyText: A good task scenario is realistic, goal-oriented, and specific enough to be measurable without revealing how the user should complete the task.
Elements.Notes: Use the framing of 'what would this person naturally want to do?' rather than 'what feature do we want to test?' This shift in perspective leads to more naturalistic and informative scenarios.

Items.Text: Task scenarios should reflect activities that real users would actually perform with the product.
Scenarios must avoid implying the correct interface path or solution to the participant.
Each scenario should have a clear, observable endpoint that defines task completion.
Tasks should be ordered from simple to complex to build participant confidence progressively.

Elements.Title: Writing Scenario Context and Prompts
Elements.BodyText: Scenario prompts include a brief narrative context that situates the participant in a realistic use case, followed by a specific action prompt that tells them what goal to accomplish.
Elements.Notes: Example: Instead of 'Use the search function to find a product,' write 'Imagine you want to buy a birthday gift for your niece who loves art. Starting from the home page, find a product you might purchase for her.' The narrative grounds the task without guiding the solution.

Items.Text: The context narrative should be brief, relatable, and free of technical jargon.
Action prompts should describe the end goal, not the steps to achieve it.
Avoid using the exact labels or terminology used in the interface within the scenario wording.
Scenarios should be written in second-person to engage the participant directly.

Elements.Title: Task Measurability and Success Criteria
Elements.BodyText: Before testing begins, teams must define what constitutes successful task completion and how partial or failed completion will be recorded.
Elements.Notes: Success criteria should be established before data collection to prevent post-hoc rationalization of results. For example: 'Task is successful if the participant reaches the confirmation page within 5 minutes without assistance.'

Items.Text: Success criteria must be defined in advance to ensure consistent scoring across participants.
Tasks can have binary success/failure outcomes or graduated completion levels.
Time-on-task is a common quantitative measure that requires a defined start and end point.
Failure conditions such as task abandonment or requests for help must also be operationally defined.

Elements.Title: Piloting and Refining Task Scenarios
Elements.BodyText: Pilot testing involves running one or more trial sessions with non-study participants to identify ambiguities, timing issues, or errors in the task scenarios before live testing.
Elements.Notes: Pilot participants should match the target population as closely as possible. Use the pilot to calibrate session timing, verify that tasks are understandable, and check that all recording and measurement tools function correctly.

Items.Text: Pilot sessions reveal unclear wording or unintended cues embedded in scenario prompts.
Timing data from pilots helps set realistic per-task time allocations during the main study.
Any changes to scenarios after piloting must be documented to preserve methodological transparency.
Team members should rotate roles during the pilot to practice facilitation and note-taking.

Elements.Title: Sequencing and the Test Script
Elements.BodyText: The test script is the facilitator's master document that sequences all tasks, instructions, and transitions in the exact order they will occur during each session.
Elements.Notes: The script should be detailed enough that any team member could run the session in an emergency. Include verbatim text for instructions, prompts, and transitions to ensure consistency across participants.

Items.Text: The test script opens with an introduction, consent confirmation, and warm-up questions before tasks begin.
Each task should appear in the script with its prompt text, success criteria, and any facilitator notes.
Transition language between tasks should be neutral and consistent so as not to prime participants.
The script closes with a post-test questionnaire or debrief to capture overall impressions.

Topics.Title: Think-Aloud Protocol
Topics.Summary: Explains the think-aloud method, its theoretical basis, and how facilitators can train participants and manage sessions to elicit rich verbal data without biasing behavior.

Elements.Title: What Is the Think-Aloud Protocol?
Elements.BodyText: The think-aloud protocol asks participants to verbalize their thoughts, decisions, and reactions continuously as they interact with the product, giving evaluators direct access to the user's mental model.
Elements.Notes: Think-aloud was formalized in usability research by Clayton Lewis and Jakob Nielsen, drawing on Ericsson and Simon's work on verbal protocols in cognitive psychology. It remains one of the most widely used methods in usability testing.

Items.Text: Think-aloud captures user reasoning in real time, revealing why errors and confusions occur.
Verbalized thoughts expose gaps between the user's mental model and the product's design model.
Think-aloud is particularly valuable for identifying interface elements that mislead or confuse users.
The method is inexpensive to implement and applicable across a wide range of product types.

Elements.Title: Concurrent vs. Retrospective Think-Aloud
Elements.BodyText: Concurrent think-aloud requires participants to verbalize during the task, while retrospective think-aloud asks them to narrate their thoughts after completing the task, often while reviewing a session recording.
Elements.Notes: Concurrent think-aloud is the standard approach for most usability studies. Retrospective is useful when vocalizing during the task would be too disruptive (e.g., time-sensitive tasks) but introduces memory bias as a limitation.

Items.Text: Concurrent think-aloud provides the richest real-time data but may slightly slow task performance.
Retrospective think-aloud reduces interference with task performance but relies on participant memory.
Some studies combine both methods, using concurrent think-aloud followed by a brief retrospective review.
Teams should select the approach that best fits their research questions and task types.

Elements.Title: Training Participants to Think Aloud
Elements.BodyText: Most participants are not naturally accustomed to verbalizing their thoughts while working, so a brief training exercise at the start of the session is essential to establish the behavior.
Elements.Notes: A common warm-up exercise is to ask the participant to think aloud while completing a simple, unrelated task such as counting the windows in a mental image of their home. This normalizes the behavior before the actual tasks begin.

Items.Text: The facilitator should explain the think-aloud protocol in plain language before the session begins.
A short practice task unrelated to the product helps participants internalize the verbalization habit.
Participants should be told explicitly that there are no right or wrong answers and that the product is being evaluated, not them.
The facilitator should model think-aloud briefly to demonstrate the expected level of verbosity.

Elements.Title: Facilitator Techniques During Think-Aloud Sessions
Elements.BodyText: During the session, the facilitator must prompt participants who go silent without interfering with their problem-solving or revealing information about the interface.
Elements.Notes: Neutral prompts such as 'What are you thinking right now?' or 'Can you tell me more about that?' are effective for re-engaging silent participants. Avoid prompts that lead the participant or suggest a course of action.

Items.Text: Neutral probes such as 'What are you thinking?' encourage verbalization without introducing bias.
Facilitators should remain poker-faced and avoid reacting to participant struggles or successes.
Never answer usability questions or confirm whether the participant is on the right track during a task.
If a participant is completely stuck, have a pre-planned assistance protocol that is applied consistently across all sessions.

Elements.Title: Recording and Capturing Think-Aloud Data
Elements.BodyText: Think-aloud sessions should be audio or video recorded so that verbal data can be accurately transcribed and analyzed after the session.
Elements.Notes: Screen recording software combined with audio capture is the most common setup for lab-based think-aloud sessions. Ensure all recording devices are tested before the session and that participants have consented to being recorded.

Items.Text: Audio-visual recordings capture verbal data, facial expressions, and on-screen behavior simultaneously.
A note-taker should document key observations in real time as a backup to recordings.
Timestamps in recordings make it easier to locate and code specific moments during analysis.
All recordings must be stored securely and handled according to the study's data privacy commitments.

Topics.Title: Quantitative Data Collection
Topics.Summary: Covers the types of numerical usability metrics, how they are measured during testing sessions, and how to design data collection instruments for consistent quantitative capture.

Elements.Title: Core Usability Metrics
Elements.BodyText: Quantitative usability metrics provide objective, numerical evidence of how well users can interact with a product, enabling comparison across tasks, sessions, and design iterations.
Elements.Notes: The HEART framework (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task Success) and the ISO 9241-11 definition of usability (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction) are useful frameworks for selecting appropriate metrics.

Items.Text: Task completion rate measures the percentage of participants who successfully complete each task.
Time-on-task records how long participants take to complete each task from start to finish.
Error rate counts the number of incorrect actions or wrong paths taken during task completion.
Efficiency metrics such as clicks per task or page visits per task provide additional behavioral detail.

Elements.Title: Standardized Usability Questionnaires
Elements.BodyText: Post-task and post-session questionnaires provide standardized quantitative measures of perceived usability and user satisfaction that complement behavioral observation data.
Elements.Notes: Commonly used instruments include the System Usability Scale (SUS), the Single Ease Question (SEQ), and the NASA Task Load Index (TLX). SUS produces a 0–100 score; scores above 68 are considered above average usability.

Items.Text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a 10-item Likert questionnaire that yields a standardized usability score.
The Single Ease Question (SEQ) is administered after each task to capture immediate perceived difficulty.
Standardized questionnaires allow comparison of results to published benchmarks and other studies.
Teams should administer questionnaires consistently — at the same points in every session — to ensure comparability.

Elements.Title: Designing Data Collection Instruments
Elements.BodyText: Data collection instruments such as observation logs, timing sheets, and error tally forms must be designed before testing begins to ensure all relevant data is captured consistently across sessions.
Elements.Notes: Pre-built data collection sheets with fields for each task, each metric, and each participant reduce real-time cognitive load on note-takers. Use digital forms where possible to streamline later aggregation.

Items.Text: Each instrument should have clearly labeled fields for participant ID, task number, and all measured metrics.
Observation logs should include columns for behaviors observed, timestamps, and facilitator prompts used.
Instruments must be piloted during practice sessions to verify they capture all necessary data points.
Digital data entry tools reduce transcription errors compared to paper-based recording.

Elements.Title: Timing and Measurement Consistency
Elements.BodyText: For timing data to be meaningful and comparable across participants, start and end points for each task must be precisely defined and consistently applied by the team.
Elements.Notes: Use a stopwatch or screen recording timestamp rather than manual note timestamps for greater precision. Define whether timing starts when the task is read aloud or when the participant begins interacting with the interface.

Items.Text: Task start and end points must be operationally defined in the test script before data collection begins.
All team members timing tasks must use the same measurement tool and apply the same start/stop criteria.
Outlier timing data caused by interruptions or technical issues should be flagged and noted, not silently discarded.
Consistent measurement practices are essential for valid within-study and cross-session comparisons.

Elements.Title: Aggregating Quantitative Data
Elements.BodyText: After all sessions are complete, quantitative data from individual participants must be aggregated into summary statistics that represent the overall study findings.
Elements.Notes: For small sample sizes typical of formative studies, use descriptive statistics (means, medians, ranges) rather than inferential statistics. Presenting individual data points alongside averages provides a more complete picture given small n.

Items.Text: Task completion rates are typically reported as a percentage across all participants for each task.
Mean and median time-on-task values summarize performance while revealing the spread of the data.
Error counts should be aggregated per task and per participant to identify both task-level and user-level patterns.
Data aggregation should be performed in a spreadsheet or dedicated analysis tool to reduce manual calculation errors.

Topics.Title: Qualitative Data Collection
Topics.Summary: Addresses methods for capturing non-numerical data during usability testing, including observation notes, verbal data from think-aloud protocols, and post-session interviews.

Elements.Title: Types of Qualitative Data in Usability Testing
Elements.BodyText: Qualitative data in usability testing includes verbal utterances, observable behaviors, emotional reactions, and participant-reported preferences that cannot be meaningfully reduced to numbers.
Elements.Notes: Qualitative data answers the 'why' behind the quantitative 'what.' A task failure rate tells you that a problem exists; think-aloud data and observation notes tell you why it exists and what users expected instead.

Items.Text: Verbal data from think-aloud protocols captures real-time user reasoning and expectations.
Behavioral observations document actions, hesitations, and navigation patterns not captured by metrics alone.
Post-task interview responses reveal user attitudes, preferences, and mental models in greater depth.
Qualitative data is essential for generating actionable redesign recommendations from usability findings.

Elements.Title: Structured Observation and Note-Taking
Elements.BodyText: Effective note-taking during usability sessions requires a structured approach that captures specific, observable behaviors rather than interpretations or evaluations.
Elements.Notes: Train note-takers to write descriptive, not evaluative, notes. 'Participant clicked the back button three times before finding the checkout link' is better than 'Participant was confused.' The former is usable data; the latter is an inference.

Items.Text: Notes should be specific, behavioral, and tied to a task or timestamp for later reference.
Observers should distinguish between direct observations and their own inferences in their notes.
Pre-formatted observation sheets help note-takers maintain consistency across sessions.
Multiple observers capturing data independently and then comparing notes can improve completeness and reduce individual bias.

Elements.Title: Post-Test Interviews and Debrief
Elements.BodyText: A brief post-test interview or debrief at the end of each session gives participants the opportunity to reflect on their overall experience and raise issues that did not emerge during task performance.
Elements.Notes: Keep the debrief to 5–10 minutes to respect participant time. Open-ended questions such as 'What did you find most confusing?' or 'What would you change about this experience?' often yield high-value qualitative insights.

Items.Text: Post-test questions should be open-ended to allow participants to introduce topics the team may not have anticipated.
The debrief is an opportunity to probe specific moments the team observed during the session.
Participants should be thanked and debriefed on the actual purpose of the study at the end of the session.
Debrief responses should be recorded or transcribed for inclusion in qualitative analysis.

Elements.Title: Affinity Diagramming for Qualitative Synthesis
Elements.BodyText: Affinity diagramming is a team-based method for organizing and synthesizing large volumes of qualitative observations into grouped themes and patterns.
Elements.Notes: After all sessions are complete, teams write each individual observation on a separate note card or sticky note, then collaboratively cluster them by theme. Disagreements about clustering are productive opportunities for team discussion.

Items.Text: Each observation is written as a discrete unit before grouping begins to prevent premature synthesis.
Clusters that emerge organically from the data are more reliable than forcing data into predetermined categories.
Affinity diagrams make it easy to identify which usability problems were most frequent or widespread.
The resulting themes directly inform the findings section of the structured results report.

Elements.Title: Documenting Quotes and Critical Incidents
Elements.BodyText: Direct participant quotes and critical incidents — moments of significant struggle, surprise, or delight — are among the most compelling qualitative evidence in a usability report.
Elements.Notes: Critical incidents are defined as specific observable events that have a noticeably positive or negative impact on task completion. Flag these during note-taking with a special marker so they can be easily located during analysis.

Items.Text: Verbatim quotes preserve the participant's own language and should not be paraphrased in the report.
Critical incidents should be documented with the task context, the behavior observed, and its apparent impact.
A collection of quotes and critical incidents makes abstract usability findings tangible for stakeholders.
Teams should cross-reference critical incidents with quantitative data to identify corroborating evidence.

Topics.Title: Conducting Live User Testing Sessions
Topics.Summary: Prepares student teams to manage the practical logistics and interpersonal dynamics of running real usability testing sessions, including team roles, session setup, and in-session facilitation.

Elements.Title: Team Roles During a Testing Session
Elements.BodyText: Each usability testing session should have clearly assigned team roles — typically a facilitator, a note-taker, and one or more observers — to ensure all data is captured without overwhelming any one person.
Elements.Notes: Roles should be assigned and practiced during the pilot session. The facilitator should not also be the primary note-taker, as managing the session and capturing detailed data simultaneously leads to gaps in both.

Items.Text: The facilitator guides the session, delivers prompts, and maintains neutral communication with the participant.
The note-taker documents observations, quotes, and behavioral data in real time throughout the session.
Observers remain silent during the session and document their own observations independently.
All team members debrief together immediately after each session to capture fresh impressions.

Elements.Title: Session Environment Setup
Elements.BodyText: The testing environment must be prepared before each session to ensure the product is in the correct starting state, recording tools are functioning, and the space is free from distractions.
Elements.Notes: Create a pre-session checklist that the team runs through before each participant arrives. Items should include: prototype or product reset, recording devices started, browser history cleared, consent forms ready, and water available for the participant.

Items.Text: The product or prototype must be reset to the same starting state before every participant session.
All recording tools should be tested and confirmed functional at least 15 minutes before the session begins.
The physical or virtual environment should minimize interruptions and external distractions.
Consent forms, screener confirmation, and session materials should be organized and accessible at the start.

Elements.Title: Opening the Session
Elements.BodyText: The session opening establishes rapport with the participant, confirms consent, explains the think-aloud protocol, and sets expectations for how the session will proceed.
Elements.Notes: The opening is critical for reducing participant anxiety and establishing the correct mindset. Emphasize that the team is testing the design, not the participant's abilities, to reduce performance pressure and encourage honest behavior.

Items.Text: Welcome the participant warmly and briefly explain the purpose and structure of the session.
Review and confirm informed consent before any recording or task activity begins.
Explain the think-aloud protocol and conduct the warm-up exercise to establish verbalization behavior.
Clarify that participants should not ask for help during tasks but can flag frustrations verbally.

Elements.Title: Managing In-Session Challenges
Elements.BodyText: Facilitators must be prepared to handle common session challenges such as participant silence, off-task conversation, technology failures, and requests for guidance.
Elements.Notes: Prepare a brief protocol for each foreseeable challenge and include it in the test script. Having pre-planned responses reduces facilitator hesitation and keeps the session consistent. For technology failures, decide in advance whether to pause, reschedule, or continue with alternative materials.

Items.Text: Use neutral prompts to re-engage participants who fall silent during tasks.
Redirect off-task conversation politely but promptly to maintain session focus and timing.
Technology failure protocols should be decided before testing begins and applied consistently.
If a participant requests help, apply the pre-defined assistance protocol rather than improvising.

Elements.Title: Closing the Session and Post-Session Debrief
Elements.BodyText: Closing the session involves thanking the participant, administering any final questionnaires, debriefing on the study's purpose, and distributing any participant incentives.
Elements.Notes: The team debrief immediately after a session — before the next participant arrives — is one of the most valuable steps in the process. Fresh, unfiltered impressions captured at this point often surface insights that get lost during formal analysis.

Items.Text: Administer the post-test questionnaire before revealing any information about the study's goals.
Debrief the participant on the actual research purpose after all data collection is complete.
Distribute participant incentives and confirm any data privacy assurances made during consent.
The team should hold a brief internal debrief immediately after the participant leaves to capture shared observations.

Topics.Title: Compiling Structured Results for Analysis
Topics.Summary: Guides student teams through the process of organizing, synthesizing, and presenting usability testing findings in a structured results document that supports actionable recommendations.

Elements.Title: Organizing Raw Data After Testing
Elements.BodyText: Before analysis can begin, all raw data from every session must be compiled, labeled, and organized in a consistent format that allows comparison across participants and tasks.
Elements.Notes: Establish a shared folder structure and file naming convention for the team before testing begins. Data disorganization after multi-session studies is a common problem that significantly delays and complicates analysis.

Items.Text: All quantitative data should be entered into a single shared spreadsheet organized by participant and task.
Qualitative notes and transcripts should be compiled and labeled with participant IDs and session dates.
Recordings should be backed up and timestamped to facilitate later reference during analysis.
Raw data files should never be overwritten; maintain original files alongside any processed versions.

Elements.Title: Identifying Usability Problems and Patterns
Elements.BodyText: Analysis involves reviewing the compiled data to identify recurring usability problems, patterns of behavior, and areas of the product that consistently caused difficulty across participants.
Elements.Notes: A problem that affected only one participant may still be worth noting, but problems observed across multiple participants should be prioritized. Frequency and severity are the two primary dimensions for prioritizing usability problems.

Items.Text: Problems observed by multiple participants are stronger evidence of a genuine usability issue than single-participant observations.
Cross-reference quantitative metrics with qualitative observations to build a complete picture of each problem.
Severity ratings can be assigned based on impact on task completion and frequency of occurrence.
Not every observation is a problem — distinguish between usability issues and individual user preferences.

Elements.Title: Structuring the Results Report
Elements.BodyText: The results report is the primary deliverable of the usability study and should present findings in a clear, logical structure that moves from study overview to findings to recommendations.
Elements.Notes: A typical usability report structure includes: Executive Summary, Study Overview (goals, participants, methods), Quantitative Findings, Qualitative Findings, Prioritized Usability Issues, and Design Recommendations. Tailor this to assignment requirements.

Items.Text: The executive summary provides a concise overview of the most critical findings for stakeholders who may not read the full report.
The study overview section documents the methodology, participant characteristics, and tasks used.
Findings sections should present evidence before conclusions, allowing the reader to evaluate the basis for each claim.
Recommendations should be specific, actionable, and linked directly to the evidence that supports them.

Elements.Title: Presenting Quantitative Findings
Elements.BodyText: Quantitative findings should be presented using tables, charts, and summary statistics that make numerical patterns immediately visible and interpretable.
Elements.Notes: Bar charts work well for comparing task completion rates across tasks. Line graphs can show performance trends across participant sequence if order effects are of interest. Avoid pie charts for most usability data — they are less precise than bar charts for comparison.

Items.Text: Task completion rate tables should include both the count and percentage of successful completions per task.
Mean and range values for time-on-task data reveal both average performance and the spread of individual variation.
SUS or other questionnaire scores should be reported alongside published benchmark comparisons where available.
Every chart and table should have a clear title and explanatory caption so it can be understood without reading the surrounding text.

Elements.Title: Presenting Qualitative Findings and Recommendations
Elements.BodyText: Qualitative findings are most effectively communicated through a combination of themed summaries, direct participant quotes, and specific critical incident descriptions.
Elements.Notes: Stakeholders are often most persuaded by verbatim quotes because they make abstract usability problems concrete and human. Pair quotes with behavioral data (e.g., 'Three of five participants said [quote] and all three failed this task') to strengthen the evidence.

Items.Text: Organize qualitative findings into themed sections that correspond to major usability problem areas.
Use direct participant quotes as primary evidence for attitudinal findings and user expectations.
Critical incidents should be described with enough specificity that a reader can visualize exactly what occurred.
Each design recommendation should be written as a specific, implementable action tied to a documented finding.
